content: Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) is the primary cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea. Its clinical manifestations vary widely, ranging from asymptomatic carriage to diarrheal illness, and in severe cases, to complications such as pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, or bowel perforation. Diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of diarrhea along with positive stool tests for toxigenic C. difficile or its toxins, or endoscopic findings indicative of pseudomembranous colitis. Treatment strategies and antibiotic selection should be tailored based on disease severity and the risk of recurrence. Diagnostic Criteria Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America (SHEA) The diagnosis of CDI should be based on a combination of clinical and laboratory findings. A typical case is defined by: The presence of diarrhea, characterized as three or more unformed stools within 24 hours or less, and A stool test positive for toxigenic C. difficile or its toxins, or colonoscopic or histopathological findings demonstrating pseudomembranous colitis. The same criteria apply to diagnosing recurrent CDI. European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) Diagnosis of CDI is based on: A combination of clinical signs and symptoms confirmed by microbiological evidence of C. difficile in stool, in the absence of another cause, or Colonoscopic or histopathological findings demonstrating pseudomembranous colitis. Diagnostic tests for CDI include: Enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) and toxins A and B. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), such as PCR, targeting 16S ribosomal RNA, GDH genes, or toxin genes. Cell culture cytotoxicity assay (CCA). Culture of toxigenic C. difficile. Classification of Disease Severity IDSA and SHEA The initial episode of CDI can be stratified by severity: Mild-to-moderate disease. Severe disease. Severe, complicated disease. ESCMID Severe disease is defined as an episode of CDI with: One or more specific signs and symptoms of severe colitis, or A complicated disease course, including significant systemic toxin effects and shock, necessitating intensive care unit admission, colectomy, or resulting in death. Severity of colitis can be assessed through: Physical examination. Laboratory investigations. Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy. Imaging studies. American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) The classification includes: Mild disease. Moderate disease. Severe disease. Complicated disease. Recurrent disease. Risk Factors The most significant risk factor for CDI is antibiotic use. Other established risk factors include: Advanced age. Chemotherapy. Chronic kidney disease. Consumption of processed meat. Contact with active carriers. Cystic fibrosis. Diabetes mellitus. Hypoalbuminemia. Immunosuppression, immunodeficiency, or HIV. Prolonged or multiple antibiotic use. Inflammatory bowel disease. Liver cirrhosis. Malignancy. Malnutrition. Residence in nursing homes or long-term care facilities. Presence of comorbid conditions. Presence of gastrostomy or jejunostomy tubes. Previous gastrointestinal surgery or endoscopic procedures. Previous hospitalization or prolonged hospital stays. Solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Use of proton pump inhibitors. Antibiotics associated with CDI include: Very common: clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins. Somewhat common: penicillins, macrolides. Uncommon: tetracyclines, aminoglycosides. Management Asymptomatic Carrier No treatment is indicated. Mild Disease Discontinuation of the predisposing antibiotic. Hydration. Monitoring of clinical status. Administration of metronidazole (500 mg three times daily). Moderate Disease Consider hospitalization. Discontinuation of predisposing antibiotics. Hydration. Monitoring of clinical status. Administration of metronidazole (500 mg three times daily). Severe Disease Hospitalization. Oral or nasogastric vancomycin (500 mg four times daily), with or without intravenous metronidazole (500 mg three times daily). Complicated Disease Antibiotics as for severe infection. Surgical consultation for subtotal colectomy or diverting ileostomy with vancomycin colonic lavage. Consideration of fecal microbiota transplantation or additional antibiotics. First Recurrence Oral vancomycin (125 mg four times daily for 14 days). Second or Further Recurrence Vancomycin in a tapered and pulsed regimen, or Fecal microbiota transplantation, or Fidaxomicin (200 mg twice daily for 10 days). Dos and Don’ts Dos Inform the laboratory when testing for C. difficile from formed stools in a patient with ileus. Initiate empiric antibiotics regardless of laboratory results when there is a high suspicion of CDI. Deliver vancomycin via enema for patients in whom oral antibiotics cannot reach a segment of the colon (e.g., Hartmann’s pouch, ileostomy, colonic diversion). Test for C. difficile in patients with diarrhea in the context of malignancy, chemotherapy, immunosuppressive therapy, organ transplantation, cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, or pregnancy. Don’ts Do not test for C. difficile in a patient without diarrhea. Do not repeat testing if the initial results are negative. Do not perform tests for microbiological cure. Do not treat asymptomatic carriage. Do not administer antiperistaltic agents to patients with suspected or confirmed CDI.
